p.src: Now Jiang Wei, while retreating, encountered Sima Shi leading troops to intercept him. It turned out that when Jiang Wei seized Yong Province, Guo Huai had sent an urgent report to the court. The ruler of Wei consulted with Sima Yi and settled upon a plan. Sima Yi dispatched his eldest son, Sima Shi, with fifty thousand troops to aid the fighting in Yong Province. Hearing that Guo Huai had repelled the Shu army, Sima Shi judged it weakened and came to strike it on the road; He pursued them as far as Yangping Pass, but Jiang Wei employed the repeating-crossbow method handed down by the Martial Marquis, concealing more than a hundred such crossbows on both sides; each discharged ten bolts, all poisoned. The crossbows on both sides loosed together, killing countless men and horses in the vanguard. Amid the chaos, Sima Shi fled back for his life.

p.src: Meanwhile, in the city of Qushan, the Shu general Gou An saw that no relief force was coming, so he opened the gates and surrendered to Wei. Having lost tens of thousands of soldiers, Jiang Wei led the defeated remnants back to Hanzhong and encamped there. Sima Shi returned to Luoyang. In the eighth month of autumn in the third year of Jiaping, Sima Yi fell ill. As his condition steadily worsened, he summoned his two sons to his bedside and charged them: “I have served Wei for many years and attained the office of Grand Tutor, the highest rank a subject may hold; Yet everyone suspects me of harboring other ambitions, and I have ever lived in fear. After my death, you two must govern the affairs of state well. Take heed! Take heed!” With these words, he died. His eldest son, Sima Shi, and his second son, Sima Zhao, reported the matter to Cao Fang, ruler of Wei. Cao Fang provided lavish funeral rites and burial, and generously bestowed posthumous honors and a title. He appointed Sima Shi General-in-Chief, placing him in overall charge of the Secretariat’s confidential affairs of state; and made Sima Zhao General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry.

You gentlemen must proceed with care.” He then ordered Wang Chang and Guanqiu Jian each to lead ten thousand troops and form up on the left and right without advancing for the time being; once Dongxing Commandery had been taken, they would all advance together. The Wei soldiers laughed loudly at the sight and made no further preparations.

All his soldiers drew their short swords, followed him ashore, and hacked their way into the Wei camp. The Wei soldiers were caught unprepared. Han Zong hastily snatched up the great halberd before his tent to meet the attack, but Ding Feng had already rushed inside his reach; with one sweep of his sword, he struck Han Zong to the ground. Huan Jia came around from the left and thrust his spear at Ding Feng, but Ding Feng caught the shaft under his arm. Huan Jia abandoned his spear and fled. Ding Feng hurled a sword after him, striking him squarely in the left shoulder, and Huan Jia pitched backward to the ground. Ding Feng overtook him and stabbed him with the spear. The three thousand Wu soldiers charged to and fro throughout the Wei camp. Hu Zun hurriedly mounted his horse and fled by whatever road he could find. The Wei soldiers all rushed onto the pontoon bridge, but it had already broken, and more than half fell into the water and drowned; countless others were cut down upon the snow. The Wu soldiers captured all their wagons, equipment, horses, and weapons. When Sima Zhao, Wang Chang, and Guanqiu Jian heard of the defeat at Dongxing, they too reined in their armies and withdrew.

p.src: Now Zhuge Ke led his troops to Dongxing. After withdrawing the army and rewarding its labors, he assembled his generals and said, “Sima Zhao has been defeated and has retreated north. This is the perfect opportunity to press our advantage and advance upon the Central Plains.” On the one hand, he sent an envoy bearing a letter into Shu, asking Jiang Wei to advance and attack the north, promising that they would divide the realm equally between them; on the other, he raised a great army of two hundred thousand and marched against the Central Plains. As he was about to depart, a stream of white vapor suddenly rose from the ground and cut across the entire army, leaving men unable to see those facing them. Jiang Yan said, “This vapor is a white rainbow, an omen that troops will be lost. Grand Tutor, you should return to the court and must not attack Wei.” Zhuge Ke flew into a rage. “How dare you utter such ill-omened words and weaken the resolve of my army!” He ordered the guards to behead him. Everyone pleaded for Jiang Yan’s life, so Zhuge Ke merely stripped him of office and reduced him to commoner status. He continued to urge the army onward. Ding Feng said, “Wei regards Xincheng as its chief strategic pass. If we take that city first, Sima Zhao’s courage will be shattered.” Zhuge Ke was delighted and immediately hastened his troops straight to Xincheng. The Gate Commandant Zhang Te, who guarded the city, saw the great Wu army approaching, shut the gates, and held firm. Zhuge Ke ordered his men to surround the city on every side. A swift courier had already carried the news to Luoyang. The registrar Yu Song advised Sima Shi, “Zhuge Ke is now besieging Xincheng, but we should not yet engage him. The Wu army has come from afar; its men are many and its provisions few. When its grain is exhausted, it will withdraw of its own accord. Wait until they are about to leave, then strike them, and we shall win a complete victory. I fear only that the troops of Shu may invade our borders, and against that we must be on guard.” Sima Shi approved his counsel and ordered Sima Zhao to lead an army to assist Guo Huai in guarding against Jiang Wei; while Guanqiu Jian and Hu Zun were sent to hold back the Wu army.

p.src: Now Zhuge Ke attacked Xincheng for several months without taking it. He ordered all his generals to combine their strength in the assault, declaring that anyone who showed the least negligence would be beheaded at once. The generals accordingly attacked with all their might, and the northeastern corner of the city was on the verge of collapse. Within the city, Zhang Te devised a stratagem. He ordered an eloquent man to carry the registers to the Wu camp and address Zhuge Ke: “The law of Wei states that when a city is besieged, if its commander holds out for a hundred days without relief arriving, then should he leave the city and surrender to the enemy, his family will not be held guilty. Your army has now besieged us for more than ninety days. We beg you to grant us a few more days; then my commander will lead every soldier and civilian out of the city to surrender. For now, we present these registers in advance.”

p.src: Zhuge Ke believed him completely, drew back his troops and horses, and ceased attacking the city. In truth, Zhang Te had used a delaying tactic to trick the Wu army into withdrawing. He tore down houses within the city and used their materials to repair the breached wall completely. Then he climbed the battlements and cursed them loudly: “We still have provisions enough for half a year. How could we ever surrender to the dogs of Wu! Come and fight as much as you please!” Zhuge Ke was furious and urged his men to storm the city. A wild shower of arrows rained down from the walls. An arrow struck Zhuge Ke squarely in the forehead, and he toppled from his horse. His generals rescued him and carried him back to camp, where the wound became severely inflamed. The entire army lost the will to fight; and because the weather was fiercely hot, many soldiers fell ill. When Zhuge Ke’s wound had somewhat improved, he wished to order another assault on the city. A camp officer reported, “Everyone is ill. How can they fight?” Zhuge Ke raged, “Anyone who speaks of sickness again will be beheaded!” When the soldiers heard of this, countless numbers deserted. Suddenly came a report that the commander Cai Lin had led the troops under him over to Wei. Zhuge Ke was greatly alarmed. He mounted his horse and inspected every camp himself, and indeed saw that the soldiers’ faces were yellow and swollen and that all bore signs of illness. He therefore ordered the army to withdraw to Wu. A spy had already carried word of this to Guanqiu Jian. Guanqiu Jian mobilized his entire army and fell upon the Wu forces from behind. The Wu army suffered a crushing defeat and fled home. Zhuge Ke was deeply ashamed and stayed away from court on the pretext of illness. Sun Liang, ruler of Wu, personally visited his residence to inquire after his health. Civil and military officials all came to pay their respects. Fearing that people would criticize him, Zhuge Ke began searching out the faults of the officials and generals. Those guilty of minor offenses were banished to the frontiers; those guilty of serious ones were beheaded as a warning to all. Thereafter every official, both within and outside the court, trembled with fear. He also placed his trusted generals Zhang Yue and Zhu En in command of the imperial guards, making them his claws and fangs.

p.src: Now Sun Jun, whose courtesy name was Ziyuan, was a great-grandson of Sun Jing, the younger brother of Sun Jian, and a son of Sun Gong. He murders high ministers and nobles and will soon harbor treasonous designs. You are a member of the imperial clan. Why do you not act against him before it is too late?” Sun Jun said, “I have long entertained that very intention. I shall report to the Son of Heaven at once and request an edict for his execution.” Thereupon Sun Jun and Teng Yin sought an audience with Sun Liang, ruler of Wu, and secretly reported the matter. Sun Liang said, “I too am greatly afraid whenever I see this man. I have often wished to remove him, but have found no opportunity. If you are indeed loyal and righteous, you may secretly devise a plan against him.” Teng Yin said, “Your Majesty should arrange a banquet and summon Zhuge Ke. Conceal armed men behind the wall hangings, cast down a cup as the signal, and kill him at the feast, thereby ending all future danger.” Sun Liang agreed.

Teng Yin said, “Your Majesty should arrange a banquet and summon Zhuge Ke. Conceal armed men behind the wall hangings, cast down a cup as the signal, and kill him at the feast, thereby ending all future danger.”
Sun Liang agreed.

p.src: Now ever since Zhuge Ke had returned to the capital after his defeat, he had remained at home on the pretext of illness, his mind restless and distracted. One day, when he happened to step into the main hall, he suddenly saw a man dressed in hempen mourning clothes enter. Zhuge Ke shouted at him and demanded an explanation. The man was so startled that he did not know what to do. Zhuge Ke ordered him seized and interrogated. The man said, “My father recently died, so I came into the city to ask monks to perform memorial rites for him. At first I thought this was a monastery and entered, never imagining that it was the Grand Tutor’s residence. How in the world did I come to this place?” In anger, Zhuge Ke summoned the soldiers guarding the gate and questioned them. The soldiers answered, “Several dozen of us have stood at the gate bearing arms and have never left it even for a moment. We saw no one enter.” Zhuge Ke flew into a rage and had every one of them beheaded. That night Zhuge Ke slept uneasily. Suddenly he heard a crash like a thunderbolt in the main hall. He went out to look for himself and saw that the central roof beam had snapped in two. Terrified, Zhuge Ke returned to his bedchamber. Suddenly a chill wind arose, and he saw the mourning-clad man he had killed and the several dozen gate guards, each carrying his own severed head and demanding his life. Zhuge Ke collapsed in terror and did not regain consciousness for a long while. When he washed his face the next morning, he found that the water reeked strongly of blood. Zhuge Ke berated his maidservants and made them change the basin dozens of times, but every basin smelled exactly the same.

p.src: While Zhuge Ke was still startled and perplexed, it was suddenly reported that an imperial envoy had arrived to summon the Grand Tutor to a banquet. Zhuge Ke ordered his carriage and attendants prepared; but just as he was about to leave the residence, a yellow dog caught hold of his robe and whined as though weeping. Zhuge Ke said angrily, “Is this dog making sport of me?” He ordered those around him to drive it away, then mounted his carriage and left the residence. Before he had traveled more than a few paces, he saw a white rainbow rise from the ground before the carriage and soar into the sky like a length of white silk. Zhuge Ke was deeply alarmed and bewildered. His trusted general Zhang Yue approached the carriage and warned him privately, “A banquet is being held in the palace today, but whether its purpose is good or ill is unknown. My lord, you must not enter lightly.” After hearing him, Zhuge Ke ordered the carriage turned around. Before it had gone a dozen paces, Sun Jun and Teng Yin rode up and asked, “Why is the Grand Tutor turning back?” Zhuge Ke replied, “I have been struck by a sudden pain in my belly and cannot appear before the Son of Heaven.” Teng Yin said, “Since the Grand Tutor returned from the campaign without an audience in which matters could be discussed, the court has arranged this banquet especially to summon you, as well as to deliberate upon important affairs. Though you are indisposed, Grand Tutor, you should make the effort to attend.” Zhuge Ke accepted his counsel and entered the palace together with Sun Jun and Teng Yin. Zhang Yue followed them inside as well. Zhuge Ke appeared before Sun Liang, ruler of Wu, performed the customary courtesies, and took his seat at the banquet. Sun Liang ordered wine to be served. Suspicious, Zhuge Ke declined, saying, “In my present illness, I cannot bear to drink.” Sun Jun said, “You habitually drink medicinal wine at your residence, Grand Tutor. Could we fetch some for you?” Zhuge Ke replied, “That will do.” He therefore sent an attendant back to his residence to fetch his specially prepared medicinal wine, and only then did Zhuge Ke drink with his mind at ease.

p.src: After several rounds of wine, Sun Liang, the ruler of Wu, made an excuse and withdrew first. Sun Jun descended from the hall, cast off his long robe, and put on short garments over a coat of ring-mail. Then, a keen blade in hand, he returned to the hall and cried aloud, “His Majesty has decreed that the traitor be put to death!” Zhuge Ke, greatly alarmed, dashed his cup to the floor and tried to draw his sword to meet the attack, but his head had already fallen to the ground. When Zhang Yue saw Sun Jun cut down Zhuge Ke, he brandished his saber and rushed to meet him. Sun Jun hastily dodged the point of the blade, though it wounded a finger on his left hand. Sun Jun wheeled around and struck with his saber, hitting Zhang Yue in the right arm. The guards surged forward together, struck Zhang Yue down, and hacked him to a pulp. Sun Jun ordered the guards to seize Zhuge Ke’s family, while also commanding that the bodies of Zhang Yue and Zhuge Ke be wrapped in reed mats, carried out on a small cart, and cast into a pit among the disorderly graves on Shizigang outside the city’s southern gate.

p.src: Now Zhuge Ke’s wife was in her chamber, dazed and deeply uneasy, unable to sit or stand at peace. Suddenly a maid entered the room, and Zhuge Ke’s wife asked her, “Why does your whole body reek of blood?” The maid suddenly glared and gnashed her teeth, leaping wildly and striking her head against a roof beam as she cried aloud, “I am Zhuge Ke! The treacherous villain Sun Jun has plotted my murder!” Everyone in Zhuge Ke’s household, old and young alike, cried out and wept in terror. Before long, troops arrived and surrounded the residence. They bound every member of Zhuge Ke’s family, old and young alike, took them to the execution ground in the marketplace, and beheaded them. This took place in the tenth month of winter, in the second year of the Jianxing era of Wu. In former days, when Zhuge Jin was still alive, he saw that Zhuge Ke displayed all his cleverness openly and sighed, “This son is not one who will preserve our house!” Moreover, Zhang Ji, Guanglu Grandee of Wei, had once said to Sima Shi, “Zhuge Ke will soon die!” When Sima Shi asked the reason, Zhang Ji replied, “When a man’s power overawes his sovereign, how can he endure for long?” And now his words had indeed come true.

p.src: Now after Sun Jun had killed Zhuge Ke, Sun Liang, the ruler of Wu, appointed him Chancellor, General-in-Chief, and Marquis of Fuchun, placing him in supreme command of all military affairs within and beyond the court. From that time onward, all power passed into Sun Jun’s hands.
